stories.headline: Peltola insists 'I knew nothing' about alleged 'Decoy Dan' scheme as Sullivan alleges she is 'still lying'
stories.note: Sullivan keeps the pressure on Peltola as the Dem-linked spoiler scheme dogs her Alaska Senate bid.
body: Alaska Democratic Senate candidate Mary Peltola told supporters in Juneau on Thursday that she had no knowledge of an alleged effort to put a second, same-named Dan Sullivan on the ballot against the Republican incumbent.

Sen. Dan Sullivan isn't buying it. In an interview with Fox News, he said Peltola is "still lying" and accused her campaign, along with Democrats in Washington and Alaska, of planning for more than a year to confuse voters.

The flap stems from a New York Times report Wednesday that Peltola's campaign and senior aides at the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee carried out the plan, hoping two Dan Sullivans on the ballot would pull votes from the senator. The other candidate, a retired schoolteacher listed as "Sullivan, Daniel J. Jr.," has been nicknamed "Decoy Dan" by critics.
The Justice Department is moving to delay certification of Alaska's Senate results because of the two Sullivans appearing side by side on the ballot.
Sullivan called it the biggest scandal in Alaska's electoral history and predicted it would have a huge impact on the race, saying, "We're not dumb."
Why it matters: A scandal tying the Democratic nominee and national Democrats to a voter-confusion scheme gives Sullivan a powerful closing message in a seat Democrats hoped to flip.

stories.headline: Trump DOJ's fight over 20K suspected noncitizen voters takes sharp turn as California ballots pour in
stories.note: DOJ is appealing to the Ninth Circuit after a judge blocked its bid to set aside ballots from 20,000 flagged California voters, keeping the state's refusal to check them in the spotlight.
body: A federal judge on Wednesday turned down the Justice Department's emergency request to make California set aside mail-in ballots tied to more than 20,000 registered voters the administration flagged as likely noncitizens.

Federal officials said Homeland Security Investigations and partner agencies used several data checks to identify the voters. California disputed the list, saying an early review turned up U.S.-born people and voters with no voting history.

U.S. District Judge David O. Carter, a Clinton appointee, said the late intervention would disrupt an election already underway, though he noted federal authorities can still pursue individual fraud cases. State officials said more than 500,000 ballots had already been separated from identifying information.

The DOJ isn't backing down. First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said the Solicitor General authorized an immediate appeal and the department will seek an emergency order from the Ninth Circuit. Election expert Hans von Spakovsky criticized California officials, saying they "don't even want to check."
On the other side, UCLA law professor Rick Hasen called the request a federal overreach, arguing states run congressional elections unless Congress says otherwise.
Why it matters: The ruling is a setback, but the appeal keeps California's refusal to verify flagged voters in the spotlight, an issue Republicans are pressing hard on election integrity.

stories.headline: Dead felon voting controversy grows as 'Betty No Last Name' surfaces in Spanberger's rights restoration push
stories.note: New questions about Gov. Spanberger's voting-rights restoration push put Virginia Democrats on defense.
body: Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger's push to restore voting rights to convicted felons came under new fire Thursday after an attorney obtained a restoration citation addressed to "Betty No Last Name."

The citation lists the recipient among more than 66,000 Virginians whose voting, jury and office-holding rights have reportedly been restored. It comes days before a Nov. 3 ballot measure that would make restoration automatic upon release from prison.

Virginia Beach attorney Tim Anderson, who got the document through a public records request to the Chesapeake Sheriff's Office, said it shows nobody actually reviewed the cases. He suspects the citations were produced by mail merge and signed by autopen, despite language saying each case was individually reviewed. The find follows reports that notices went to felons who have died.

Former Attorney General Jason Miyares piled on, saying Spanberger's "individualized review" may be "just imaginary." State Sen. Glen Sturtevant, who wants an independent audit, urged voters to reject Question 3.
Why it matters: The episode hands Republicans a vivid example of sloppy oversight right before Virginians vote on making felon rights restoration automatic.

stories.headline: Feds raid multiple Minnesota autism service providers amid Medicaid fraud investigations
stories.note: Federal raids widen the Medicaid fraud scandal in Democrat-run Minnesota.
body: Federal agents raided several Minnesota autism service providers Thursday, the latest action in a state already under heavy scrutiny for fraud in taxpayer-funded programs.

The FBI confirmed court-authorized activity at multiple sites in the Twin Cities and Rochester. The operation involved the FBI, HHS's inspector general, IRS criminal investigators, postal inspectors and Minnesota's Bureau of Criminal Apprehension. Attorney General Keith Ellison's Medicaid fraud unit also served warrants at two providers in St. Louis Park and Edina.

One of them, Iska Inc., received more than $16.7 million in Medicaid payments from 2018 to 2025, according to state data reviewed by the Star Tribune. The state's autism intervention program has drawn mounting fraud concerns, with DOJ saying its Medicaid claims jumped from about $600,000 in 2018 to over $400 million by 2025.

The searches follow 22 warrants executed in April and charges against 15 defendants in May tied to alleged schemes with more than $90 million in intended losses. No charges have been announced from Thursday's raids, and the allegations remain unproven.
Why it matters: The raids come just ahead of Vice President JD Vance's planned visit with the White House fraud task force, keeping the Walz-era fraud scandal front and center before Election Day.

stories.headline: Minnesota official's voter guide message on Somali TV triggers viral backlash: 'Not an accident'
stories.note: A Minnesota official's Somali TV voter message sparks a viral backlash.
body: A clip of Minnesota's voter outreach director, Melanie Hazelip, explaining voting rules on Somali TV of Minnesota has gone viral and reignited election-integrity concerns.

In the Oct. 26 appearance, Hazelip told viewers that registered voters don't need to bring anything to vote early, and that unregistered voters can sign up the same day with an updated Minnesota ID or other documents. Her remarks matched state law, but the post shared by End Wokeness drew close to a million views.

Critics noted that Minnesota issues driver's licenses regardless of immigration status, with no citizenship marking, and lets a registered voter vouch for up to eight others. Retired Navy intelligence officer Phillip Parrish wrote that the system's ease "is not an accident." Riley Gaines said it shows why the SAVE America Act is needed.
The Secretary of State's office said Hazelip gave accurate information and that her remarks were "misinterpreted and misrepresented by political actors online."

Bill Glahn of the Center of the American Experiment said that, given the timing and the audience, she should have stressed that only citizens can vote, pointing to a noncitizen recently sentenced in the Feeding Our Future fraud.
Why it matters: Coupled with the state's fraud scandals, the clip fuels Republican arguments for tougher voter-ID and citizenship checks heading into Tuesday.

stories.headline: Cruz says there's 'real risk that Americans will die' if El-Sayed gains access to US intelligence
stories.note: Cruz sharpens the GOP case against Michigan Democrat El-Sayed in a key Senate race.
body: Sen. Ted Cruz, campaigning in Michigan on Wednesday for Republican Mike Rogers, warned that Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed could pose a national security danger if elected.

Cruz argued that nothing would stop Chuck Schumer from putting El-Sayed on the Senate Intelligence Committee, which handles the country's most sensitive secrets. He said that if El-Sayed is a supporter of the Muslim Brotherhood, as Cruz believes, "there is a very real risk that Americans will die."
Cruz pointed to U.S. troops and undercover operatives working against terrorists and claimed El-Sayed might tip off targets about to be apprehended.

El-Sayed told Bret Baier last week that he has "never been" and never will be a Muslim Brotherhood member and that he wants to serve the United States. Neither campaign responded to Fox News Digital on Thursday.
Why it matters: Cruz's appearance puts national security at the center of the GOP's closing pitch in Michigan, where Trump-backed Rogers is trying to flip an open Senate seat.

stories.headline: Nearly 40 House Dems skip effort to end Ilhan Omar immigration probe
stories.note: Dozens of House Democrats declined to back the push to shut down the Omar probe, showing cracks in the caucus.
body: Nearly 40 House Democrats stayed off a letter, led by Rep. Pramila Jayapal, demanding the Trump administration end its investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar's immigration paperwork.

About 175 Democrats, over two-thirds of the caucus, signed. But former Speaker Nancy Pelosi and former Majority Leader Steny Hoyer did not, and neither did several Democrats in tough races, including Henry Cuellar, Tom Suozzi, Marie Gluesenkamp Perez and Don Davis.
The letter argued the probe could sway voters in Omar's district a week before the election and accused officials of weaponizing law enforcement.

Investigators are examining whether Omar or her father misstated her birth year to obtain citizenship after the family fled Somalia. Agents searched her home on Oct. 12 under a judicial warrant, taking phones and notebooks. Omar calls it a political attack.
Why it matters: Vulnerable Democrats keeping their distance shows the Omar case is a liability they don't want to own heading into Election Day.
